source.title: Fine-Tune, Then Rectify
source.authors: Zikun Ye; Jinglong Zhao; Lei Wang

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper and online appendix are present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests power-law scaling in a new setting: fine-tuning or supervised adaptation measured by labeled-sample count and residual variance, rather than pretraining loss measured against model parameters, tokens, or compute.
record.gate_note: The paper's own fitted curves for residual variance versus fine-tuning sample count are included. Cited pretraining scaling-law results are not rows. The allocation experiments concern splitting human labels between fine-tuning and rectification, not allocating a fixed compute budget between model parameters and pretraining tokens. Other estimator comparisons and performance metrics are omitted unless they report a scaling-law result or fit sensitivity.
record.test_reason: The study fits its own power law, a·s^-α + b, to held-out residual variance against the number of labeled fine-tuning samples. The model is an MLP head trained on frozen text-embedding-3-large embeddings. This is a new training regime (supervised adaptation on downstream labels) that bears on V5. It also reports fit sensitivity across datasets and resamples, which bears weakly on V7. It does not vary model size, pretraining tokens or compute.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is essentially correct. The authors conclude that residual variance of their fine-tuned surrogate follows an empirical power law in labeled sample size, and that this law guides the optimal split of labels between fine-tuning and PPI rectification. They also conclude that a variance-based fine-tuning objective beats MSE. Model size is explicitly held fixed, and the paper's 'fine-tuning' is mainly an MLP head on frozen embeddings.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures held-out residual variance during downstream fine-tuning or adaptation as labeled sample count changes. Its main mean-estimation model uses frozen embeddings and a trained MLP head; it also reports an affine calibration case and a supplementary LoRA check. It does not sweep pretraining model parameters, pretraining tokens, or compute, or use held-out pretraining cross-entropy.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported task-specific exponents differ across the Wine Reviews mean-estimation and clothing-review mean-estimation fits. For the Wine Reviews fit, bootstrap refits disperse in individual parameters while the allocation ratio remains concentrated; one-shot early-size fits vary in selected allocation, with relatively modest predicted interval-width costs.

fits_no_version.finding: The optimal label allocation between fine-tuning and PPI rectification, derived from the fitted law, is stable under bootstrap but varies from 10% to 28% under one-shot fits. The interval-width cost is modest because the objective is flat near its minimum.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Decisions derived from small-sample fine-tuning scaling fits are robust to fit noise when the downstream objective is flat near its optimum.

fits_no_version.finding: An affine calibration of a zero-shot LLM output has a slope-weighted residual-variance curve that fits a power law (adjusted R2 = 0.98) over 50–3,000 labels.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Residual variance of low-dimensional calibration of LLM predictions decays as a power law in calibration labels.

record.problems: The principal Wine Reviews curve is based on a single dataset and task; it uses a fixed foundation-model size and measures residual variance rather than pretraining cross-entropy. The clothing curve uses five measured development sizes. The price-rating fit's power-law coefficients are not reported in the supplied text. Some fit-sensitivity and robustness results concern the paper's label-allocation objective rather than pretraining scaling.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows. The paper's label-allocation results, estimator comparisons, LoRA single-allocation comparison, and cross-entropy-objective comparison do not report another power-law sweep for the claim versions cataloged here.

untested.parts: Image and video models; repeated data; transfer; full or LoRA fine-tuning of a language model across sample sizes (the LoRA check is a single allocation); scaling with model size in any non-text-pretraining regime.

Dependence of pretraining exponents on parameter counting, schedule or fitting method; disagreements between published laws; the compute-optimal parameter/token split; whether the training objective (variance vs MSE) changes the fitted exponent (no fitted MSE curve is reported).
Not tested: no pretraining loss against parameters, tokens or compute.
Not tested: there is only a short extrapolation below the measured grid (s*=141 at n=1,000), not an extrapolation over orders of magnitude.
Not tested: model size is held fixed.

missing.what: Validation residual variance across s for variance-loss vs MSE-loss training. Variance loss is consistently lower, most of all at small s. This shows the training objective shifts the curve, which is relevant to V7, but no fitted parameters are reported for MSE.

The residual-variance response curve for directly concatenating the zero-shot prediction with the raw embedding stays above the zero-shot baseline until about s=3,000. The parameterization changes how the curve behaves; full curves are only in the replication materials.
The share of fit variability from data sampling vs training randomness is 18%–46% from data sampling, depending on the quantity.

record.verdict_notes: The study's 'scaling law' concerns a downstream regression head, or a linear calibration, on frozen LLM features. It treats the published LLM scaling laws as motivation and does not test them; the cited Kaplan and Hoffmann results are not rows. Its bearing on V5 is weak: the system is not a language model being fine-tuned, and the only LoRA result is one matched pair at s=1,135. The V7 evidence is about estimation noise and dataset differences, not controlled fitting-choice comparisons. The text contains no instructions.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining cross-entropy as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Extrapolating pretraining-loss power laws from small runs to runs orders of magnitude larger.
The compute-optimal parameter/token allocation, including how either count scales with pretraining compute.
Comparisons of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Image and video models, repeated data, transfer beyond the reported applications, and whether the same form holds for pretraining cross-entropy in other modalities or regimes.
Downstream task performance as a function of model scale or pretraining loss.

Dependence of pretraining-law exponents on parameter counting, pretraining schedules, or fitting methods; disagreements between the cited pretraining laws; curvature in pretraining-loss curves; and the compute-optimal parameter/token split.

rows.subject: frozen text-embedding-3-large model with an MLP regression head
rows.stage_stated: MLP head trained on labeled reviews; embeddings frozen
rows.operation_detail: Fit residual variance against the number of fine-tuning samples using the variance-based objective.
rows.measure: Held-out residual variance Var(Y − f(X)) versus fine-tuning sample count s
rows.uncertainty: 95% error bars; 1.96 standard errors over the replicates
rows.note: The authors describe the power law as closely fitting the measured response. Figure points are medians over ten training replicates per size.
rows.check: Link and state are correct. The system is a two-layer MLP head on frozen embeddings, not a fine-tuned language model, so V5 bears only in a probe-style adaptation regime. Adjusted R2 = 0.999 over the measured sizes.

rows.subject: fine-tuning specification using the gpt-5.6-sol text-only zero-shot prediction
rows.stage_stated: Labeled-data affine adaptation: c0 + c1 p + c2 fzs(X)
rows.operation_detail: Fit a power law for the slope-specific, price-weighted residual variance across fine-tuning sample sizes.
rows.measure: Slope-specific variance criterion Var(p[Y − f(X)]) versus fine-tuning sample count
rows.value: Power-law fit with adjusted R2 = 0.98; allocation rule selects s*=318
rows.note: The fitted power-law coefficients are not stated. The paper reports that the objective is within 1% of its minimum for allocations of approximately 180 to 550 labels.
rows.check: The 'fine-tuning specification' is a three-coefficient affine calibration, c0 + c1 p + c2 fzs, of a zero-shot LLM output. This is linear-regression estimation error, not neural fine-tuning scaling. The fitted coefficients and exponent are not reported, so the row cannot speak to the power-law form for V5 or V7. The value 's*=318' is an allocation output, not a scaling result.

rows.subject: frozen text-embedding-3-large model with an MLP prediction head
rows.stage_stated: MLP head trained on labeled clothing reviews; embeddings frozen
rows.operation_detail: Fit residual variance against development sample count using variance-loss training.
rows.measure: Residual variance versus fine-tuning sample count
rows.note: The fitted exponent differs from the reported Wine Reviews mean-estimation fit; these are different tasks and datasets, not a controlled comparison of setup choices.
rows.check: The fit uses only five measured development sizes. The range of s is not stated.

rows.subject: frozen text-embedding-3-large model with an MLP regression head
rows.stage_stated: MLP head trained on labeled Wine Reviews; embeddings frozen
rows.operation_detail: Refit the fine-tuning residual-variance law under hierarchical bootstrap resampling of datasets and training seeds.

conditions.value: 1,200 hierarchical draws from 10 datasets and three seeds per dataset

rows.measure: Fitted law parameters and implied optimal fine-tuning allocation ratio
rows.value: Median a = 14.265, α = 0.391, b = 2.338; 95% robustness intervals [10.057, 63.832], [0.251, 0.531], and [0.990, 2.434], respectively; median s*/n = 0.104 with 95% interval [0.094, 0.107]
rows.uncertainty: 95% robustness intervals from the hierarchical bootstrap
rows.note: The paper reports dispersion in individual parameter estimates but a more concentrated allocation ratio.
rows.check: Remove the V5 link: this is a robustness refit, not a separate setting. For V7 the relevant fact is the exponent: α ranges 0.251–0.531 across data and seed resamples, and the bootstrap median of 0.391 differs from the full-grid 0.318. The 'baseline' is the allocation ratio, a quantity derived from the label-allocation rule, not a scaling-law quantity.

rows.subject: frozen text-embedding-3-large model with an MLP regression head
rows.stage_stated: MLP head trained on labeled Wine Reviews; embeddings frozen
rows.operation_detail: Fit the scaling law using one training run at each of four small development sizes, then compare the selected allocation with a reference fit.

conditions.value: single run at each size; repeated for ten runs

rows.measure: Sensitivity of selected allocation and predicted confidence-interval width to a one-shot fit
rows.baseline: Reference law fitted to the other nine runs
rows.value: At n = 1,000, selected allocation ratios range from 10% to 28%; median predicted interval-width increases range from 0.3% to 5.3% across tested budgets, with a maximum of 10.4% across runs and budgets
rows.note: Using six sizes up to 2,000 reduced median increases to below 3% at every budget, with a maximum of 7.9%.
rows.check: This row measures the sensitivity of the selected label allocation and the confidence-interval-width cost to one-shot fits. It reports no fitted exponents and is not a compute-optimal split. It concerns the paper's own allocation method rather than the scaling law's form.

relationships.condition: MLP regression head on frozen text-embedding-3-large embeddings, trained with the residual-variance loss; Wine Reviews and clothing-review rating prediction
relationships.reason: Held-out residual variance against labeled sample count fits a saturating power law closely (adjusted R2 0.999 in R1, 0.963 in R3). This holds only for probe-style head training, not language-model fine-tuning.
relationships.display_finding: Held-out residual variance fitted saturating data power laws with adjusted R² of 0.999 for Wine Reviews and 0.963 for clothing reviews.

relationships.condition: Across datasets and tasks (Wine vs clothing reviews), with the same pipeline
relationships.reason: The fitted exponent changes greatly with data: α=0.318 in R1 vs 1.213 in R3. The floor b differs as well (2.17 vs 0.393). This is a different-task comparison, not a controlled one.
relationships.display_finding: Wine and clothing review tasks yield α values of 0.318 versus 1.213 and loss floors b of 2.17 versus 0.393, although task differences prevent a controlled attribution.

relationships.condition: Wine Reviews; hierarchical bootstrap over 10 data draws × 3 seeds
relationships.reason: Individual parameters disperse widely: α interval [0.251, 0.531] and a interval [10.1, 63.8] in R4. The bootstrap median α=0.391 differs from the full-grid 0.318, so the fitted exponent depends on the data sample and seed. The fitted curves themselves stay clustered.
relationships.display_finding: Bootstrap intervals span 0.251–0.531 for α and 10.1–63.8 for a, with median α=0.391 versus the full-grid 0.318, while fitted curves remain clustered.
